questions.q: What does SQL Server use as its boolean idiom, since it has no true BOOLEAN column type?
options: CHAR(1) storing 'Y' or 'N'
BIT, storing 0, 1, or NULL
TINYINT(1), the same as MySQL
A native BOOLEAN type identical to PostgreSQL's
questions.explain: SQL Server has no BOOLEAN column type; BIT (0/1/NULL) is the idiomatic stand-in.

questions.q: What are the two traditional conventions Oracle developers use for a boolean-style flag column, given that Oracle historically had no boolean column type?
options: A native BOOLEAN type and TIMESTAMPTZ
BIT and TINYINT(1)
CHAR(1) with 'Y'/'N', or NUMBER(1) with 0/1
VARCHAR2 storing the literal words 'true' and 'false'
questions.explain: CHAR(1) ('Y'/'N') and NUMBER(1) (0/1) are the two traditional Oracle conventions for a flag column.

questions.q: What does MySQL's BOOLEAN type actually resolve to under the hood?
options: It resolves to CHAR(1), matching Oracle's convention
It's literally an alias for TINYINT(1), not a distinct type
It's a fully distinct type enforced separately from any integer type
MySQL has no BOOLEAN keyword at all
questions.explain: MySQL's BOOLEAN/BOOL is purely an alias -- querying the column's real type reveals TINYINT(1).

questions.q: Which platform in this lesson has a genuine native BOOLEAN type with real true/false/NULL values enforced by the type system?
options: MySQL
Oracle
PostgreSQL
SQL Server
questions.explain: PostgreSQL is the one exception here -- a true native BOOLEAN type, unlike the other three platforms.

questions.q: Where does PL/SQL's BOOLEAN type apply, and where does it NOT apply?
options: It applies equally to both table columns and procedural code
It exists for use inside procedural code, but historically could not be used as a table column type
PL/SQL has no BOOLEAN type anywhere
It only applies to table columns, never inside procedural code
questions.explain: PL/SQL's BOOLEAN works inside procedural code but historically was not usable for storing table column data.
